utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seric, are you ready for your closing argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honour Judge Clark, Judge Diarra, Mr. Scott, Mr. Stringer, Mr. Poriouvaev, Mr. Bos, good afternoon. Good afternoon, everybody in the courtroom. In my life, I took the oath twice. The oath of a Judge in distant 1978 and the oath of a lawyer in 1995. Different and yet basically the same, that I shall never place myself in the way of the justice. I was a Judge in a first instant court and I was a Judge in the appellate court. I was never a Prosecutor. I have to tell you, Your Honours, that as somebody who read law, it was a surprise to me to hear how impotent was the Prosecution in corroborating their claims, their inability to provide you with evidence, Your Honours. They said on the contrary that the Defence has not proven its claim, the Defence has not proven the innocence of Vinko Martinovic and I must say that it is nonsense. I have not yet heard in my practice and it is not an accident. It is not an error. I have realised that this is a constant and permanent conduct of the Prosecutor from the opening to the final brief. I've accused them, you have to judge them, and the Defence is merely in the way. I hope you will forgive me, Your Honours, gentlemen in the Prosecution, but I'll be in your way a little bit more. The story does not start with the disintegration of the former Yugoslavia on the 25th of June, 1991, as is claimed by the Prosecutor. The story starts a long time before that and it is not the disintegration of the former Yugoslavia and it is not an error in this regard. It is an error concerning the creation of Yugoslavia. The story starts in 1918 with the Versailles treaty when the kingdom of the Serbs, Croats and Slovenes came into being, subsequently termed Yugoslavia. A despotic autocratic kingdom of Yugoslavia which in fact represented Serbia. So this former tiny kingdom in the Balkans believed that it had a right to expand into the territories of other states which fell apart at the end of World War I: The Austria Hungarian empire and the Turkish empire. The territory where for over a thousand years other peoples have been living without the right to independence and national sovereignty. Your Honours, one must first address facts indicating that the Office of the Prosecutor substitutes the thesis regarding the causes of the conflict, the immediate cause, and the effect so as to presumably in the name of the international community and in point of fact in the name of the extremist part of the Muslim state party SDA and their leader Alija Izetbegovic, persistently trying to offer us the thesis on the position of the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina as exclusively victims and the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina as a betterance of the Republic of Croatia and its army. The time before the beginning of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina is characteristic of the preparations of parties for the war. The intensity of those preparations was not always even, especially because the initial stage was different. The Serb Democratic Party took the lead, a Serb party which was supplied with weapons by the Serbified JNA. And the Croats through the HDZ also came by some weapons but in significantly smaller quantities than the Serbs; however, sufficient to gradually reduce the feeling of inferiority after the JNA disarmed the republican Territorial Defence. With Muslims, their situation was the least favourable, partly because they found themselves between the rock and the hard place of various leaders and political parties, yet they started making steps in this regard at a very early stage. They formed the Muslim Patriotic League in May 1991, and at that time, one can -- they could be considered only as a party military formation. In that arms -- that arms race involved the ethnic principle too, because everybody was arming on his own behalf, from the Serb ethnic areas, which in 1991 and 1992 -- which were the place where the JNA had pulled out its material and its forces from Slovenia and from Croatia, from these territories the Serbs started to expand their territories. They achieved successes in eastern Bosnia in areas with the majority Muslim population, in the area of the south western Bosnia, apart from the successes in Kupres, the Serbs suffered dual failure in Croat territories and areas. They failed in their attempt to take Sarajevo and in the valley of the Neretva, and towards the end of March, hard fighting started and lasted for several months to conquer Bosanska Posavina. In the area of Bosanska Krajina where there was no major resistance, the practice of ethnic cleansing started and the establishment of concentration camps; a practice which shortly expanded into other parts of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In contrast with the Serbs, the first stage of the war in the case of Croats and Muslims passed in an attempt to consolidate the defence front lines. Within that context, the significance of Croat successes strategically outweighed the successes of the BH Army for very simple reasons. The -- Croatia followed because it served for both of those threatened people the logistics bases and support. The engagement of the Croatian Army, that is the ZNG along the northern and southern borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina, with a mutual support of the HVO, also meant direct support to the BH Army in depth because they tied up some of the Bosnian Serb forces in these engagements and enabled the logistics and humanitarian support. And in regard to this fact, one can see collective amnesia, not only in Bosnia-Herzegovina but in Croatia too. When Jajce and Bosnian Posavina fell, the war of the Croat Defence Council against the army of Republic of Serbia literally came to an end, having defended Livno, part of the Vrbas valley, and parts of central Bosnia and especially after the successes in the Neretva valley, crowned by the June dawn, the HVO more or less reached a stalemate with the Serbs. And after that there was only some positional fighting, the occasional exceptions being Usora and parts of the Posavina theatre of war. Several meetings between the leaders of Bosnian Serbs and Croats outside the BH did not yield any specific results. We heard in this courtroom that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had the least reason to be happy. Towards the end of 1992, it controlled the -- it had the weakest ratio between the number of the population and the area under its control. The structure of that Bosnian regime in which their party, the SDA, predominated and the HDZ was its subordinate partner, expedited disintegration of the Bosnian state. Right until January 1993, Sefer Halilovic blamed Croat politicians for the conflict between the HVO and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is also important to mention that on the 20th of May, 1992, the HVO was officially considered an integral part of the BH Army, and the Tudjman-Izetbegovic agreement of July that same year recognised the Croat Defence Council and the BH Army as separate components of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina that would be linked up through their joint staff. However, a political rift between these two armed forces took place. They split in two parts, the HVO as the Croat force and the BH Army as a party army of the SDA under an increasingly pronounced Muslim predominance. The Islamic patriotism or religious patriotism were synonymous with the Bosnian struggle for liberation, the formations of the 7th Muslim Brigade and the black swans were nevertheless more radical in their Islamic fundamentalist motives. And these formations provided the basis for a parallel chain of command used by Izetbegovic and his confidant Hasan Cengic. On the 18th of March, 1992, Boban, Karadzic, and Izetbegovic, under the auspices of Cutilheiro adopted the declaration on the principles of the new constitutional order and it says: "Bosnia-Herzegovina should be an independent state made of three constituent entities based on ethnic principles." Your Honours, the conflict between the Army of BH and the HVO, that struggle was the struggle for Lebensraum. The Serbs had captured over 60 per cent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and expelled Bosniaks and Croats. Bosniaks found refuge mostly in central Bosnia and thus significantly upset the demographic balance and a settlement of the Bosniaks in areas where the Croats were a majority were -- was seen by the political and military leadership of the HVO as taking the territories away from Croats, so a conflict in Gornji Vakuf ensued. However, even during the fiercest clashes, the cooperation in many joint theatres of war never stopped. From Orasje in the north of Bosnia through the area of Tuzla, in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps of the BH Army, down to the Sarajevo theatre of war, and, Your Honours, this shows best the nature of non-international armed conflict. If one looks at documents produced by the Defence, D2/60, D2/61, D2/62, D2/63, D2/64 and D2/65, it becomes obvious that the Republic of Croatia helped the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in materiel and in manpower. So not only a rhetorical but also factual and legal question arises. Is it not true that the Republic of Croatia was also involved on the side of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? The crucial question is: Had the Republic of Croatia wanted and desired to undertake any form of aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina, would it have then proceeded to arm its future enemy? The open Muslim-Croat conflict which marked 1993 was preceded by something that dates back to the earliest days of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. For instance, at the Public Security Service in Bugojno, the war militias were issued with ammunition but only the members of Muslim ethnicity, and they were told to conceal that fact from the members of Croat ethnicity. In Gornji Vakuf, there was a tension between the Croats and the Muslims. It seems that it was precisely in the area of Uskoplje, that is in Gornji Vakuf, the first conflict between the HVO and the Territorial Defence broke out, and it was as early as late April 1992, and that it was repeated on the 20th and 21st of June, 1992. In the beginning of May, it -- a conflict broke out in Busovaca and it was repeated the next month. In Novi Travnik, a conflict took place and there was also interethnic tension in Konjic; and then in early August, a conflict broke out -- the conflict broke out in Kiseljak. Yet, at that first stage of the Muslim-Croat intolerance, a special place belongs to the 17th of August, 1992, when the units of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina broke into a Croat locality of Stup in Sarajevo. That incident was different from earlier conflicts, and one is therefore justified to ask at which level, at which Tier of responsibility was this conflict caused. The chronology of the conflict, which the public knows, starts with the conflicts in Prozor. The conflict was predicted and planned by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The deterioration of the security in the area of central Bosnia -- in central Bosnia, found its reflections regularly in the peripheral areas of the operative zone of northwest Herzegovina. And on the 21st of October, 1992, the main staff of the HVO reported that in Gornji Vakuf and Prozor the situation was tense and that a clash could break out at any time, at any moment. In the light of such situation, in a part of the operative zone, all of the security measures available were undertaken in order to prevent a conflict between the forces of the Croat Defence Council and the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially in Gornji Vakuf and Prozor. However, the conflict broke out on the 23rd of October and ended in a complete rout of the local BH Army's units. The claim that it was the HVO which had launched a surprise attack on BH Army units in Prozor is a pretty bold one, but is based on a prejudice. At a meeting of HVO and ABiH representatives of the 6th of November, 1992, in Jablanica, the representatives of the BH Army agreed to -- agreed to go along with a request of the HVO to replace the commander of the municipal staff of defence in Prozor, and that fact is not without significance when in the analysis of the conflict. Another serious problem in the relations between the HVO and the BH Army is the existence of two parallel political and military structures in the central part of Bosnia and north-east Herzegovina. There is dual authority. However, the major problem was the result of the Serb conquests and ethnic cleansing, because vast numbers of refugees and displaced persons poured from those territories into the areas controlled by the BH Army and the HVO and it upset the ethnic structure and the balance between the members of two different groups. Namely, most of the expelled persons came from the rural environment into the urban environment, urban milieu, bringing with them a completely different mind set and way of life. It is not important -- it is important to say that towns and cities had multi-cultural experience with Mostar at the forefront of such experience. This was, however, not the case with the rural areas so that especially in Mostar, not only the ethnic and demographic balance but even the balance in traditions and customs was also upset. After the Geneva talks, the political and religious leadership of the Bosniak Muslims in Mostar issued the Mostar Warning in January 1993, supporting Alija Izetbegovic and rejecting the concept of the -- of confederation. The Muslims of Herzegovina are on their own turf and everybody should be clear about it, the letter says. It also says that it is imperative for the Bosniaks and for the Bosniaks and Muslims to divide Herzegovina into three ethnic provinces. This letter was signed by Zijad Demirovic on behalf of the SDA, mufti of Herzegovina, Hadzi Sead Efendi Smajkic, and attorney Faruk Cupina the President of the Muslim council of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And it is then that the tension and ever-more frequent conflicts take place. The Muslims use zolja to hit a van with HVO troops. Arif Pasalic, commander of the 4th BH Army, announces on the Radio that Mostar will be liberated from the non-Muslim population. And what else is this but the strategy of the ethnic and religious cleansing policy? According to the instructions of the political and military leaders, the Bosniaks, Muslims, leave the Croat Defence Council and the front lines intercept HVO soldiers, harass them, inflict injuries on them, and seize the personnel and HVO property. Fear spreads amongst the non-Muslim population, tension is incited, and the rift in the HVO between the Croats and Bosniaks Muslims. The operative plan for the attack on West Mostar and its surroundings is prepared. The command of the 41st mechanised Brigade orders to prepare for combat on the 20th of April, 1993. This order is signed by Midhat Hujdur as the commander. The order said that the BH Army formations were to get ready to engage in the area of Cekrk, to close the communication Rodoc-Mostar, provide support to the 2nd Battalion in the area of Benka secondary school, Avenija Rudnik and in the parking lot at Bijeli Brijeg, Rondo, and on the university grounds. The operative plan against targets on the right bank of the Neretva was developed down to the least detail. The beginning of the conflict between the BH Army and the Croat Defence Council in Mostar took place on the 8th of May, 1993; however, the preparations started as early as March and April, 1993, Your Honours. Davor Marijan our expert witness testified about it. We have also seen documentation corroborating this. It was then when the Bosniak Muslim forces launched a fierce attack on the Tihomir Misic HVO barracks. And the very next day, General Sefer Halilovic, the Commander of the Main Staff of the BH Army in Zenica announced the final -- the definitive showdown with the Croats. Nevertheless, the real conflict broke out in the early hours of the morning of the 30th of June, 1993, between half past 2.00 and 3.00 in the morning, when Muslims, members of the Croat Defence Council, in the area of Bijeli Brijeg turned their rifles away from the Serb aggressors and on to the Croats. I believe that it has been accepted that during the course of, and at certain stages of the events in the former Yugoslavia, there were one or more international armed conflicts. And it is submitted that these conflicts co-existed with one or more internal armed conflicts, the last of which was the conflict which involved my client, Vinko Martinovic. Further on, while it has been accepted that an internal armed conflict can turn into an international armed conflict, the Prosecutor did not prove beyond reasonable doubt that facts exist in this case that there were grave breaches of Geneva Conventions and as reflected in Article 3 of the Statute of this Tribunal. The Appeals Chamber, Your Honours, in Prosecutor versus Tadic, clearly drew a distinction between an internal armed conflict which turns into an international armed conflict, and an international armed conflict which co-exists with an internal armed conflict which may or may not turn into an international armed conflict, depending on some variables. I'm not going to comment on the decision of this Chamber; we can all look at it ourselves. It is clear that the general provisions of the Geneva Convention apply only to international armed conflicts in the sense of conflicts between states or conflicts in which one state occupies the territory of another state. We all know the meaning of provision -- of the provisions of Article 2 of the Geneva Conventions. Although it is believed that individuals who represent a non-state organisation may be responsible for grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions as participants in an international armed conflict, we submit, Your Honours, that this is only the case in which such an organ is the alter ego of a state and that it represents the state, it acts on behalf of the state. The Prosecution's purported distinction from the case of Nicaragua versus United States is not legally relevant, and whether or not the intervention is a direct or not, the legal question remains the same, and that is: Was Vinko Martinovic, as the accused, acting on behalf of a party to an international -- to the conflict? The purpose of the principle of unity of identity is to establish that a state is indeed the party in question. The Appeals Chamber in Prosecutor versus Tadic did not reject the basic principle which is in conformity with the findings in the U.S. versus Nicaragua, only the specific test to be applied. It is submitted that the Prosecution has failed to establish beyond all reasonable doubt that the HVO was acting on behalf of the Republic of Croatia in the sense of having overall control over those forces at the relevant period and in the conflict in which my client, Vinko Martinovic, participated on the front line in Mostar. On the contrary, the evidence suggests, Your Honours, that the HVO participated on behalf of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in its own right, as a non-state entity. That organisation cannot be completely identified to the Republic of Croatia, and it is different from it. While it has been accepted that an international armed conflict might emerge from an internal armed conflict where the troops of a state intervene in the internal armed conflict, it is submitted that only those entities or individuals acting on behalf of a state may indeed be parties to that international armed conflict. Individuals acting on behalf of a non-state entity, this includes Vinko Martinovic, will continue to act within the context of an internal armed conflict which develops in parallel to the international armed conflict. And as such, these individuals could not be held responsible in terms of the general provisions of the Geneva Conventions. Not only do we believe but we also claim, Your Honours, that the Prosecution has failed to establish beyond all reasonable doubt the intervention of the troops which act on behalf of a state within the zone of conflict where Mr. Martinovic was on the front line. In any event, such an intervention would not have affected Mr. Martinovic's legal status in the conflict zone, since he acted on behalf of a non-state entity and therefore he could not represent a party to the conflict in terms of the provisions of the Geneva Conventions. Moreover, the Prosecution has failed to establish beyond all reasonable doubt that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna acted on behalf of the Republic of Croatia, as opposed to having acted on its own behalf in the context of a specific war in which Mr. Martinovic also took part. The fact that assistance was given to -- by a state to a non-state entity does not imply that such a non-state entity can be identified with the state. Indeed, as testified by Davor Marijan, and we also have proof that such assistance was given to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this doesn't imply the unity of identity. The international humanitarian law draws a distinction between two kinds of civil wars: A non-international armed conflict of a high intensity, Article 3, protocol 2; and other internal conflicts which are exclusively subsumed under Article 3. If there is an internal conflict, there is no -- there are no legal grounds for the application of the Geneva Conventions on the protection of victims of war. There is a sentence to that effect in the Tadic case. How should one treat the BH Army forces? Were those forces -- and they certainly were a party to the conflict, were those forces legal armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina? The answer is positive; the answer is yes. Was the HVO, as the other party to that same conflict, a legal armed force of the -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina? The answer is positive; the answer is yes. Were the -- another crucial question. At the relevant time, the time relevant to the indictment, were the alleged victims, alleged with regard to the indictment but also factual but -- because they were factual victims, so were the alleged victims citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina? The answer is positive; the answer is yes. And we have, Your Honours, positive answers to all these three questions. Then it is impossible to -- absolutely impossible to apply the 4th Geneva Conventions since Article 4 says: "This convention protects persons who, at any moment or in any way, find themselves in an instance of a conflict or occupation in the hands of a party to the conflict in the hands of a party to the conflict or an occupational force that they are not citizens of." The Geneva Conventions of 12 August, 1949, in the common article provide some criteria for the existence of a non-international armed conflict, which this Court has ignored in the case Prosecutor versus Blaskic as a mere formality and something of no importance. We believe that this ignorance will be rectified by the appeals court. According to that article, Article 2, in order for an international armed conflict to come into existence -- I don't know whether this has been heard before this Chamber, Your Honours -- there has to be a will to wage a war, and animus belligerendi. Animus belligerendi on the part of at least one party to that conflict. Such a will, not even in 1993, was shown or declared by either Bosnia and Herzegovina or the Republic of Croatia. They did not declare that they were in the state of international armed conflict with the other side. Already, in 1992, Bosnia-Herzegovina declared that it was in the state of war with Serbia, Republika Srpska, and the Serbian Democratic Party. And that was the cause for this conflict to be pronounced as an armed conflict between Bosnia and Herzegovina and the socialist federative Republic of Yugoslavia and this was pronounced in the case Prosecutor versus Tadic. Why does it concern us? It concerns us because in the relations between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia, there was never such a declaration on the part of any of the sides. Also, you have to bear in mind, Your Honours, that there are some criteria which exist in the classic war law, according to which it can be fairly reliably established whether an armed conflict has come into existence between two sovereign states, which it didn't in this case. In such a situation, it would be normal for both sides to terminate their diplomatic relations. However, Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina have maintained those relations ever since 1991, when they established them and when they mutually recognised each other. So these diplomatic relations have never been terminated, they were not terminated even during the conflicts between the BH Army and the HVO. Moreover, in an international armed conflict between two states, some kind of bilateral international contracts are either suspended or cancelled, but you can verify it has been published in all the official gazettes, both in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Croatia - we have those, they have been delivered to us by the Prosecution - several bilateral contacts between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina were signed in 1992, in 1993, and later on, and they continued to be observed. Moreover, the following question has never appeared. Citizens of one state in the other outside military operations were never treated as the citizens of a hostile state. The Prosecutor presented evidence to that effect. It was the Prosecutor, not the Defence, Your Honours. Neither BH citizens in Croatia were treated as enemies. They were extended all the help, humanitarian help, as any other refugees. Likewise, the citizens of Croatia, where the legal authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina were still active, like for example in the besieged Sarajevo or in the region of Tuzla, were not treated as the citizens of a hostile state. The situation was somewhat different in the areas which were affected by the armed conflicts. However, this only corroborates the Defence claimed that it -- the war was a civil war. Besides, trade relations were neither abolished or -- nor terminated, which would also be typical of an international conflict. Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, if they were indeed waging a war against each other, would it not have been logical that all the trade relations stopped? However, this did not happen. Your Honours, another interesting question pertaining to international war law which has not appeared in this courtroom and it always appears whenever there is an international armed conflict. The Republic of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina never undertook any acts to confiscate the moveable property of the other state. The Defence submits that all the time, throughout the war, a distinction was maintained between the Croatian Army and the military component of the HVO, and there were also different insignia on the uniforms. What leads to a certain confusion is the presence of soldiers who had previously been soldiers and officers of the Croatian Army and who joined the HVO. These were, however, citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, persons who were born in Bosnia and Herzegovina and who returned to their home state after the war had ended in Croatia, in order to fight the aggressor. The following witnesses testified to that effect: Slobodan Praljak, Bozo Rajic, Witness NB, Milan Kovac, Zeljko Glasnovic, Witness NE, Witness NM, Witness NO, Witness NP, and expert witness, Davor Marijan. In the course of 1993, indeed, certain HV units were sent to the areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina where they participated in some war operations in very small members. However, not in Herzegovina. And they never engaged in any acts of authority which would have been essential for an occupational force. If the Croatian Army units had launched an aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina, if they had been an occupier, then they should have engaged in exercising some sort of authority in the areas where they were. However, not only the Prosecutor did not provide evidence to that effect, but the Defence proved that the contrary was the fact. So it cannot be said that this presence was occupation. As regards protected persons, we believe that the victims of the alleged crimes cannot be considered protected persons for the purpose of the 4th Geneva Convention, since the alleged perpetrator, Mr. Martinovic, was not acting on behalf of a party to the conflict and it was not an occupation. This arises clearly from what I have just said. The Defence cannot admit that Vinko Martinovic acted in the context of an international armed conflict, and that is another rhetorical question. And since Mr. Martinovic could not -- did not need to be aware of the legal nature of the conflict, it is respectfully submitted that the Prosecution has failed to prove that Mr. Martinovic knew of the circumstances giving rise to an international armed conflict, and therefore, he could not have the appropriate mens rea for offences in terms of Article 2 of the Statute. As far as command responsibility is concerned, we respectfully submit that the doctrine of command responsibility applies only to commanders in armed conflicts between states, and it cannot be applied to a superior in a non-state entity involved in an armed conflict with another non-state entity. This conclusion necessarily arises from the fact that command responsibility is a doctrine pertaining to customary international law, and that the Prosecution has failed to show the practice and opinio juris which would support the extension of that doctrine to such a conflict. Moreover, we submit that the Prosecution has not proven beyond all reasonable doubt all the essential elements of command responsibility. And while there is a common practice supported by opinio juris which supports the principles of command responsibility which are applied to armed conflicts between states or armed conflicts in which one state occupies the territory of another state, the practice accompanied by the opinio juris for conflicts between non-state entities and a state or a non-state entity within the territory of one state, has not been established. The Prosecutor has not proven the common and general practice to extend these principles in the following way. We believe that the principle nullum crimen sine lege has to be applied. And that the count for command responsibility is not based on facts. Likewise, we respectfully submit that the Prosecution has failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt the essential elements of command responsibility. The Prosecutor has not proven beyond any -- all reasonable doubt the relationship between the superior and the subordinate which would reflect the de jure and the de facto effective control. In the absence of a normal military structure of education and of a command chain, we submit that what should be applied is the principle that is applied in the case of civilians which also do not belong to a traditional military organisation, and are not subordinated to the customary discipline and obligations arising from that discipline. We submit that in the case of a commander who doesn't belong to a national army, the principle of command responsibility has to be applied in a limited sense. That is, the elements of that principle have to be interpreted in a restrictive way and established by unambiguous evidence and not only through inference. It is suggested that the Prosecution has failed to satisfy this beyond all reasonable doubt. The burden of proof lies with the Prosecutor, and it is up to him to establish beyond any reasonable doubt that there is a real possibility of control over the alleged subordinates. We believe that the extension of the responsibility of the superiors to a quasi-military unit depends on whether the Prosecutor has proven beyond all reasonable doubt such a degree of control of the superior which would be similar to the control of the superiors in a normal military structure. This has been established by the committee on international law with regard to civilians and it has been accepted by the -- this Tribunal in the Celebici case and in the case of Bagilishema before the trial for Rwanda, and such a position is a guideline. But not only that, it also serves for this principle to be applied within the limits of the international customary law which is firmly established on the practice of the military conflicts between national armies. As regards the civilians -- as civilians, I would like to remind the -- Your Honours, to pay attention to the position of the Trial Chamber in the Celebici case. There are testimonies to that effect before this Trial Chamber by Witnesses MM, MN, MO, MQ, MS, and MT, who were all soldiers under the command of Vinko Martinovic. However, that has also been confirmed by the Prosecution witnesses, Allan Knudsen and Witness Q who slept in a civilian flat not far from the base of the unit and this was also confirmed with Witness NO, who issued immediate orders to the accused Vinko Martinovic. It is submitted that the Prosecution has failed to prove beyond all reasonable doubt that Vinko Martinovic, in his capacity as the commander of a small unit, who had the task to defend only one stretch of a very long street, that as such, he had the possibility to control the activities of his unit in a manner comparable to a proper military commander, save when those troops were with him on front line. The evidence shows that after the fighting the troops could put their arms aside, or some of them could even take their rifles home, and then they were absolutely beyond Vinko Martinovic's control. Likewise, the Prosecution has failed to prove beyond all reasonable doubt that when the men moved away from the front line, Mr. Martinovic had any effective control over them. Furthermore, the Prosecution has not proven that the alleged crimes were committed by men under Mr. Martinovic's command. The Prosecutor relies heavily on allusions to Stela in inverted commas. We've heard this, Stela this, Stela that, Stela here, Stela there. However, very few of those witnesses said Vinko Martinovic. And it is not accidental that that was so. The Defence has produced adequate evidence to introduce reasonable doubt concerning the hearsay statements of persons claiming to have worked under Stela, then also, further on, even in the absence of evidence of the improper use of Stela's name. The mere reference to that name, or rather nickname, is insufficient proof to satisfy this Tribunal beyond all reasonable doubt that the perpetrators operated under Mr. Martinovic's command. One would have to establish exactly who those individuals were and through independent evidence to establish that those -- to establish that such individuals were indeed under Mr. Martinovic's command. Testimonies of Witnesses AA, BB, QQ, WW, YY, MM are totally unreliable and may not be the foundation for establishing guilt beyond all reasonable doubt. On the other hand, if the Prosecution relies only on allusions or references to the nickname, that is to Stela, then one is left wondering whether such allusions are based on a general command relationship or perhaps some other motive. Your Honours, please, pay attention to testimonies by Witnesses AA, BB, EE, QQ, and MM which were intolerant, one-sided, and partial testimonies. I will quote two obvious examples. Those others I analysed in our written final brief. Well, then, Witness QQ, told us a strange story about some prisoner Karso which is completely inconsistent with what other witnesses said, and it is also inconsistent of the statement of that same witness which he gave to this Tribunal on the 18th of March, 1999, because he never mentioned that event on that occasion. That same witness describing his past military activities, said he couldn't remember the HVO units that he belonged to. He could not remember its commander. And when referring to Vinko Martinovic, he said that he saw him in different places and on various occasions. However, he described neither the circumstances nor gave us any specific information about that. He was unable to locate the building which housed Vinko Martinovic's unit's headquarters, and he was even unable to describe it, however vaguely. And the location where he said that the alleged murder of Ziko Karso had taken place, that location was never in the area of responsibility of the Vinko Skrobo unit. The same witness, QQ, described how that same day, that is 26th of July, 1993, an incident, the 26th of July, Your Honours -- an incident took place involving uniformed detainees armed with wooden rifles which is completely inconsistent with all the other evidence produced by the Prosecution referring -- addressing that particular event and notably, the testimony of Witness AF. At the same time, he could not give a single -- the name of a single detainee with those wooden rifles. He said that they had been killed but could not say where. At a later stage, he recalls some names but they did not match the names produced by the Prosecutor through Witnesses OO, PP, and IJ. Moreover, Exhibit P434 on its page 3 shows that on the 26th of July, 1993, not a single group of detainees worked anywhere in the area which made part of the zone of responsibility of Vinko Martinovic's unit. And after all, it has never been established whether this man, Ziko Karso, ever existed at all. Where is his body? How has it disappeared, and where? There is not a single shred of evidence that the Prosecution could produce -- come up with. But it is important to know that Witness QQ had his first contact with Prosecution investigators whilst in prison as a prisoner, and shortly after that he was released from this prison, which adds further doubt regarding the credibility of his testimony. Witness MM talked about an event which took place on the 29th of September, 1993, when she was allegedly evicted from her flat, after which she was taken to the separation line and then sent free to the east side of Mostar. And that that had allegedly been done by members of the unit under the command of the accused Vinko Martinovic. It is incredible, Your Honours, and I put it to you, it is absolutely unbelievable that somebody could come to the door of a flat, expel the flat, expel the tenants, resort to force, and even introduce himself at that. It would be the same as if a bank robber, for instance, burst into a bank and pointed his arms at tellers and then looked at the camera and said, "Hands up, this is a bank robbery, turn over all the money and everything that you have in your safe. Look at me, I'm Branko Seric, I'm John Smith." The Defence says something like that does not happen in real life; it defies all logic. So the reasonable doubt remains that that incident ever took place, not to mention that it happened -- not to mention the way as described by the witness. Defence witnesses testified about the misuse of the name of Stela, and this makes us doubt reasonably whether those persons indeed were under his command at the time when crimes were committed. Furthermore, if we take that the evidence of the Prosecution about subordination and -- is true, which the Defence does not accept, such evidence is nonetheless not sufficient to affirm that there was a command relationship, that is a relationship between a superior and subordinate, between Vinko Martinovic and the alleged perpetrators. We also deem that the Prosecutor has failed to prove beyond any reasonable doubt that the accused had any specific knowledge about the injuries inflicted by his subordinates. The Prosecutor relies on statements about Stela but he has not proven that Vinko Martinovic could know that his name was being used in this manner. In itself, this makes us doubt and this is -- such doubts are further encouraged by witness statements who said that Stela's name was frequently used by those individuals even when they were not truly under his command. This is indicative of a reasonable doubt as to whether the Prosecutor's evidence really has to do anything with Vinko Martinovic. Witnesses MM -- Witness MM, you can find all the pages quoted in our written, final argument. Witness MN, Witness MO, Witness MQ, MS, MT also confirm that there were instances when different groups misrepresented themselves, impersonated other groups, when engaging in the persecution of Muslims and plunder of their flats. This is also corroborated by document P626 and by Witnesses NO and NV. We also deem that the Prosecution omitted to prove that Martinovic knew or had reason to know about injuries, and I'm referring to the position of the Chamber in the Celebici case, but you have it all quoted in our final argument in its written form. We believe that the Defence has proven that there was reasonable doubt as to the existence of knowledge of offences committed by Mr. Martinovic's subordinates. That is, whenever Mr. Martinovic learned anything about that, such information did not indicate his subordinates. Under Article 28 of the Statute: "In order for persons not actually effectively acting as military commanders to be criminally liable for the acts of subordinates, it must be established that the superior either knew or consciously disregarded the information clearly indicating that his subordinates committed or were about to commit such crimes." We deem that this principle has been adopted -- is proper and it was applied correctly by the -- by the Tribunal in the case of Kayishema, prefect, holding the position of civilian leadership in a Rwandan Prefecture. In the case of civilian leaders, or leaders of a military type, but who do not command in actual or in effective military way, the Prosecution had to demonstrate first beyond all reasonable doubt that the accused had the necessary information at his disposal, and secondly, that information was clearly based on the indication that breaches of international humanitarian law had been committed, and this information clearly showed that the commission of international -- that the offence -- that the violations of international humanitarian law had been committed by his subordinates. However, the Prosecutor has failed to prove items 3 and 4, as we have just shown. And at any rate there is reasonable doubt as to whether all these elements took place. Although the third item concerned -- the third element of command responsibility concerns the omission; it is up to the Prosecutor to prove it. That is, the Prosecutor needs to prove beyond any reasonable doubt that there were such circumstances. We deem that the Prosecutor not only has failed to prove beyond any reasonable doubt that the accused had failed -- had omitted to take the necessary steps relative to the violations of international humanitarian law. The Defence, on the contrary, has indicated the reasonable doubt and has offered also clear proof showing that Vinko Martinovic did not sit calmly after receiving such information, but quite the reverse, that he actively did what he could to see that his name would not be implicated in any such case. Mr. President, I don't know whether we shall have a break now or when shall we have it? Because I'm moving to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will break here and we'll resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seric, I was advised by the interpreters that you have to keep space of your delivery, because they had a hard time to follow you. You may proceed, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. I do apologise to the interpreters. However, since the time is restricted, and we've lived with this restriction since the 10th of September last year, we tend to forget about the interpreters. Because of that, I do apologise to them. I will try to treat them more correctly and to slow down, and yet we have to finish it by the end of this day, because after me, Mr. Par will also have his final argument. Your Honours, I shall be very brief speaking about the persecutions, and I will say that the lack of any discrimination on the part of my client is best illustrated by Witness NO. He testified about -- he testified that criminals imitated Stela and did not discriminate between groups when plundering. He said that literally those criminals did not loot or expel only the Muslims; they did it to Croats too. When describing the attack on a bus, he said, and I quote, "When the old woman realised that they were Croats, she said, 'My children, my sons, we are Croats too,' and one from the group answered, 'Sit down, you hold hag. Nobody is asking you whether you're a Muslim or Croat. This ain't no population census.'" The Defence claims that Vinko Martinovic never had any discriminatory intent and the Prosecutor did not produce any evidence to demonstrate that the accused even knew the general context within which his alleged offences took place and the kind of connection between his acts and the general context. Furthermore, the Prosecutor has failed to offer a single proof that Vinko Martinovic ever identified himself with the ideology, policy, or plan on -- in the name of which the alleged crimes were committed or even that he supported them, let alone that he consciously took the risk of participating in implementing such ideology, policy, or plan. We, in particular, Your Honours, wish to point out the fact that Vinko Martinovic was just a plain soldier, and you have seen evidence to this effect. As such, he commanded a small -- the smallest unit in the HVO, which was responsible for the smallest possible part of the separation line. He did not cooperate at all with the authorities. He never, not once, attended a single meeting, be it a political or a military meeting. He is an individual who only has primary education and has no knowledge as to what is ideology, what is policy, what is a plan, let alone the character of some ideology or a policy. And he never, absolutely never, ever, received an order that would have to do with ideology, policy, or plan in the name of which the would be crimes, the alleged crimes, might have been committed. The Defence has been proving and we have proved the absence of mens rea of the criminal intent on the part of the accused, the absence of the discriminatory intent, through witnesses who were down to the last -- who were Muslims down to the last one, witnesses whom Vinko Martinovic helped in different ways throughout the war, both he and members of his family. This is also confirmed by all the soldiers in the unit that he commanded. And the absence of the discriminatory intent was also testified to by Mr. Zoran Mandelbaum, president of the Jewish community in Mostar. Your Honours, I have to address a detail which was brought up the day before yesterday -- before yesterday. It was a complete failure, but it amounts to a provocation when the Prosecutor draws a line of equality between Franjo Tudjman and Slobodan Milosevic, when he draws a sign of equality between the Serb aggression and the Croat defence and he said himself that he was representing the interests of the international community, because then we have to ask ourselves what are we talking about when the Prosecutor allegedly on behalf of the international community speaks about the deceased as if he were a living witness, then even if he put it mildly, it lacks taste, and one cannot even justify it buy the cynicism of the closing argument. Obviously, he is sorry that the man is deceased, not because he has -- he respects the dead but because he cannot charge him. The deceased is not the only witness for the Prosecution. The witness also brings up the name of Janko Bobetko whom we neither saw nor heard in this case, and the Prosecutor says that Janko Bobetko affirms that our expert witness is lying. This intent of Prosecutor to disqualify a witness who testified here before you is so dangerous that it does not exist legally. I mean it lacks complete probative value. So I wonder, Your Honours, is there a single court on earth that would venture to accept such line of thinking and such rhetoric as a conclusion and include it in -- and include it in your judgement? This is a setup, Your Honours, par excellence. When we speak about the international community, Your Honours, it is absolutely certain that the international community could have stopped the war at any given time because it obviously had enough strength to do it. And when the Prosecution says that it is representing the interests of the international community, we still do not know what is the definition of this term, its term. The Prosecutor has shown repeatedly that in point of fact, this interest was the interest of one party to the conflict, namely the Muslim side. The chief interest, the object of protection, should always, however, be man, and the principle -- and the main ethical principle should be: What you do not want done unto you, do not do unto others. But look at the double yardstick of this international community as represented in the Security Council of the United Nations. Almost half of the members do not want a permanent international criminal court. Why? There are few wars which the international community could follow on television day by day, as was the case with the wars in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, and yet, in spite of such media presence, unheard of until that time, and the fact that the war in Croatia and especially in Bosnia-Herzegovina has not been studied systematically either by historians or by sociologists who would, regardless of all sorts of experts who paraded before this Court, give a complete and composite insight into the backdrop of this war in order to draw from this practical lessons that would raise the level of understanding about the political options and thereby bring about a March objective and more just, more fair decision of this Court. Your Honours, do not remain at the level offered to you by the Prosecution. It is a one sided, a lop-sided picture, unobjective, and I will even venture to say biased, partial, so much that it represents the option of the SDA and Alija Izetbegovic. A realistic understanding of this war and especially the conflict between the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and HVO is an important element to be included in your future judgement. Regrettably, your judgement will follow -- law will come about long before all the official documents in archives of all parties to the conflict and especially in the archive of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina become available to us. And this will really make your job much harder but precisely because of that, think why this part of documentation is not available to us. I put it to you that this is because it -- you would clearly see that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina is not an innocent lamb, that the Muslim party to the conflict was not a victim but a culprit, and even in relation to the HVO, the one who started the conflict. All wars, including the one which is the subject of this case, are basically similar, from the point of view of the nature or unchangeable physiognomy. And therefore, one can easily recognise in them, even perhaps in different combinations, the violence, and above everything else, Clausewitz's paradoxical trinity of wars which according to him is made of the age-old violence, hatred, and hostility which can be viewed as a blind, natural force, the interplay of chance and probability within which the creative spirit can move freely and elements of subordination which are the instruments of policy, which make the war subject exclusively to reason. Some historians tried to affirm that the war in Croatia and the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina was caused by the allegedly untimely recognition of Slovenia, Croatia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina by the international community. Believe me, that is not true. These wars were the result after well-planned and long time prepared policy which corresponds -- which suited the local political needs in Belgrade. There were several causes why the international community didn't understand all that, all that that had existed and that had happened in Yugoslavia. Many saw Tito's Yugoslavia as the only successful model of the third way, and a multi-cultural idyll. All of a sudden, primitive ethnic nationalists started to destroy that, and against the globalising world, they wanted to create claustrophobic villages to suit their primitive interests. Some people saw the former Yugoslavia as a complex state, a movie-like state, in which the frames of the east, of the west, the north, and the south, the Latinic and the Cyrillic mosques and churches, and customs and cuisines replaced each other with a tremendous speed, where coffee could be had at one place and only 100 kilometres further down, one could have a Dalmatian food. But this view did not take into account all the relevant sociallogical elements. There was no need to dispel that myth of a good life. Regardless of what your judgement may be, Your Honours, one cannot confine members of one people into a unitarian state. There is no marriage without a mutual wish to stay married. There is no marriage without mutual respect, the respect for one's individuality, for one's identity, for one's integrity. If somebody is being abused, then that person cannot be happy and marriage will fall through, and there is no truth or there is no governor or there is no high commissioner that can save such a marriage. Can we then hope, Your Honours, that reason will -- common sense will prevail? Because common sense is what we have in common. Common sense is what penetrates the nature, and we can work to change and create nature. We can use its laws and we can create tools. Everything in nature is different and one person differs from another by gender, by the colour of his skin, strength, age, and although common sense is what makes a man a man and it exists in all people, still there is difference in the strength, the speed, and the quality of human reactions. The consciousness is the product of the common sense. Its level and degree differ from one person to another. And the material conditions of life, the religions and other ideologies, the class distinctions also shape a human being. A child, when born, becomes a slave or a free person, is a German or English or an Irish or a Croat or a Serb a Catholic or a Methodists or an Orthodox, and for those reasons, one group persecutes another, deprives it of its right. And for that reason, formally and actually for material financial interests, bloody wars have been waged. Unfortunately, when one learns history at school, one learns about when wars happen. One learns about the history of wars. And we unfortunately are here today because one such war. Unfortunately I say, but again I believe that common sense will prevail because it is the common sense that makes us accept differences among people as natural and historical facts, but at the same time to oppose and reject every theory and practice which discriminate a human being as a human being. A human being has the right to cherish his differences. Your Honours, before this Tribunal, before this Chamber, the Prosecution brought a number of witnesses who were nationally and religiously biased and who had a one-sided interest. For example, Witness O is the political leader of Muslims - the Prosecutor himself said so - and his credibility was questionable. And his world view is of Islamic fundamentalism. Sead Smajkic was not a brave man, as the Prosecutor said. He is a religious preacher and he wanted to be a leader and he thought that by publicly testifying here, he would be able to manipulate his future. And he, by testifying here, he sent a message to his Muslim brothers. These same witnesses, when they were in the position to decide whether to charge Martinovic or not, and since he was the only one who is being tried for the conflicts in Mostar, there is a tendency to charge him with everything that happened in Mostar, and the Prosecutor buys that and I thought so, until two days ago, when he delivered his closing argument. Today, I see that it was not that he bought that story but that it is a part of his world view, a part of his thinking, when in his closing argument, he showed us the footage of Jeremy Bowen, in which he showed us that people were crossed a wooden bridge in Mostar, at the same time we hear shooting, and in which it says that on the other side of the river, Vinko Martinovic was standing with his people as if there had been nobody else there but Vinko Martinovic. Then I dare say that this is nothing but propaganda, worthy of John Wayne and his role when he played a Vietnam war hero. But in this case, we don't know who the Viet-cong is, who American soldiers are, and maybe the Prosecutor himself wanted to play John Wayne's role. And when the Prosecutor said that if Vinko Martinovic had not had discriminatory intent then he should be released, Your Honours, but this is exactly what the Defence claims and says. Release this man. Let him walk free. Your Honours, you are a Trial Chamber of the United Nations of the world community, which applies law by force through you. A human being, as soon as he was created, was persuaded by the snake to eat fruit from the tree of good and evil. We have all had that fruit and all of us here in the courtroom have to live with our evil and with our good, and we are always tempted. Please show common sense. Don't show any -- that you were influenced by the prejudices that the Prosecution wanted to instill in you. Please be professional and have a cool head. Your Honours, the crimes can only be committed with a direct intent. They cannot be done as an accident, and we have managed to prove that such an intent has not existed in the accused, there was no mens Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 16779 to 16784. rea. Vinko Martinovic was a common foot soldier, without any particular role in the war, without any rank in the military hierarchy. He had the lowest level of responsibility. His actions were limited to a very narrow front line. His only guilt was that he took a rifle and he went to fight, to fight for his street, for his neighbourhood, for his house and for his people. He really loves his people; believe me when I say that. He loves his native town of Mostar, but also he respects all of his neighbours in Mostar, Bosniaks, Muslims, Serbs, Jews, and others alike. And they themselves have testified to that effect in this case. He defended himself when he was attacked, regardless of who it was who attacked him. I believe, Your Honours, that you have satisfied yourselves that my client is a very ordinary man, that he only completed elementary school, that he refused any rank, that he believed that the most honourable thing was to be a foot soldier and nothing else. I believe that you were able to fully see the role of my client in the unfortunate conflict between the BH Army and the HVO, and that our evidence was enough to create such a picture for you, although we have had many more witnesses who could have additionally confirmed that the truth is what the Defence has been able to prove. Our client has addressed you, Your Honours, in a letter in which he opened your -- his soul to you. He presented some of his personal views, and he expressed his belief that you would understand that his only guilt was that he belongs to a people, to the army of that people, which had a legitimate right to defend its territory from the aggressor, from any side it may have come. Your Honours, in the history of war waging, there were always attackers and those who were attacked. And those people who didn't know how to and who didn't have the skill to defend themselves, have disappeared in the course of history. A little while ago, Your Honours, we witnessed the situation in which Carla Del Ponte, the chief Prosecutor of this Court, declared on the 4th of October of, 2002, that she had some means available to her and that she -- her only goal is the fair and expeditious criminal Prosecution, and that for that reason, she had reviewed everything available to her in the light of the global strategy of the Prosecution, and with regard to the investigations and criminal prosecution. The Prosecutor declared that my client belongs to a group of those at a lower level of responsibility and as such, does not suit the new criteria set out by the new strategy of the indictment, and that is why she issued a request to withdraw the indictment, that the Prosecution raised against Zoran Marijanovic. Your Honours, imagine that if the Prosecutor had those criteria before, then Vinko Martinovic, a common foot soldier, and just for a brief period of time a commander of the lowest unit in the military system, then Vinko Martinovic would not be here today, I wouldn't be addressing you today, you would have never seen him. He would simply not be accused. Your Honours, you have to bear in mind, you have to simply bear in mind, that every day policy, regardless of who it is about, whether it is the day-to-day policy that will decide who will appear as accused before this trial, it seems that the answer to that question is yes. I hope that something like that, such policy, will not influence your final decision, that it will not be either the day-to-day policy or prejudices that will influence your decision. Patrica Wald, the Honourable Judge of this Court in an interview to the Croatian news agency said that there are misconceptions about this Tribunal as an institution which is supposed to build the norms of international law. According to her, this Tribunal should only deal with political and military leaders, such as Milosevic, Karadzic, and Mladic. The Prosecutor also said the other day that our -- that if we were in Mostar, and if the new strategy was applied, then yes we would be in Mostar and my learned friends caught -- I should tell you that the courtroom would be full, but it is for us to speculate and only speculate who would it be who would be sitting in the courtroom. True, the truth against lies seems like an easy fight. Because according to a proverb, the truth always wins, but is it really so? Is it really so all the time? The Defence had at its disposal the truth, but only the truth. We did not have a single document. For example, we asked from the office of President Mesic, the Office for Cooperation with this Tribunal, from the BH authorities, we asked for all of them to send us some documents, but we have never -- never -- received anything. The notorious transcripts which have appeared before this Trial Chamber, the Office of the President of the republic have had them at their disposal. However, there is not a single conversation, a single meeting, at which he was present. He made a selection and he has delivered them at his own will, and in that way, the President of the Republic of Croatia, Stipe Mesic, contaminated these transcripts as evidence. When witnesses started arriving and arrived throughout the case, that is Prosecutor's witnesses, and when we confronted them with the different things that they said, and when overnight, all of a sudden, they remembered what had happened eight or ten years ago, and when we confronted them with the truth, then we were not allowed to do so, and we wanted to do -- to use the truth because that is all that we had. So why did the Prosecution call these witnesses? When cross-examining these witnesses and when we tried to discredit them, then we were not allowed to do so, as if they were bears in the Yellowstone Park. Why? Because they were victims, as if victims don't lie. In my professional career, I was the President of a Trial Chambers, and believe it or not, I can corroborate that by statistics that I have prepared, in over a thousand cases, there were at least that number of victims with their families. And in every case, those victims lied or at least exaggerated. One has to be blind not to see that this has also happened in this case. There were a number of instances when we showed documents to witnesses which contradicted their words, and then the question can be raised whether it is the documents who are false or whether it was the witnesses who lied. According to the Prosecution, everything is possible; two things can co-exist at the same time in the same place. This is contrary to the laws of physics. This is only possible if one applies tricks and black magic. When the documents provided to us by the Prosecution were exculpatory, then those documents were proclaimed false, then these documents were not speaking the truth. And when they were charging the accused, then the documents were okay. They were true. Do you remember, and I believe you will remember, Your Honours, what Isabella said to Lord Angel in Shakespeare's Measure for Measure?
