utterances.text: Well, we will have that checked at a later stage. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will pronounce such a judgement against Shakespeare. [interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: “No ceremony that to great ones ‘longs, Not the king’s crown, nor the deputed sword, The marshal’s truncheon, nor the judge’s robe. Become them with one half so good a grace As mercy does … Why, all the souls that were, were forfeit once; And He that might the vantage best have took, Found out the remedy … I would to heaven I had your potency … …I would tell what ‘twhere to be a judge, And what a prisoner. So you must be the [first] that gives this sentence, And he that suffers. O! it is excellent To have a giant’s strength; but it is tyrannous To use it like a giant.” End of quote from Shakespeare. And finally, Mr. President, Your Honours, Judge Clark and Judge Diarra, put aside the politics that I myself have burdened you with. Put aside the international community that I've tried to portray for you and I have burdened you with that as well. Put aside the policies of the new states which have emerged from the former Yugoslavia. Put aside the presidential transcripts. Put aside the late Franjo Tudjman, Gojko Susak, Mate Boban, let them rest in peace. Put aside history. Put aside the fixation of the Prosecution by some banovina, Alija Izetbegovic, his understanding or misunderstanding of the historical, sociological, cultural aspect of our small people in our small state or states. The time is now and today to look at our client and look at him and nothing else but him and his case. He really hasn't got anything to do with any of these things. He is here by accident. Denude the accusations against Vinko Martinovic, and when you see that there is no fabric to those accusations, that there is no fabric, that there is nothing around these accusations, then you will see, and you will have to say, the emperor is naked. None of the things that Vinko Martinovic has been charged with have been proven beyond all reasonable doubt, and you have to apply the in dubio pro reo principle and you have to set him free. Do you know, Your Honours, that in Croatia and in Herzegovina, this trial -- this Tribunal is always compared with Dante's inferno and it is said that whoever enters here should forget all hope. So whoever is charged by The Hague will be convicted and will be convicted hard and long, and the Prosecution wants to prove that. And the Prosecution is asking for 35 years for Naletilic and 25 years for Martinovic. Please convince us that there is hope for those who appear before this Tribunal. Give us hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Pa?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my learned friends, I wish to speak about Vinko Martinovic, Stela, and acts that he's charged within the indictment and the evidence produced during the case. I wish to speak from the point of view of the accused, in a way, in which Vinko Martinovic might address this Court if he were -- if he came out to testify. I believe that will be the language understandable to this Court. If you ask me why Vinko Martinovic is not testifying himself, the answer is that that is because he trusts us and believes that we, his defenders, will convey his words and because he does not want to answer the Prosecutor's questions. He does not want to compete with the Prosecution. He does not want to think about traps in leading questions. He does not want to put himself in a situation where he might be provoked by false allegations. And we understand him. As his defender, I will try to present his view on every count of the indictment, because I also believe in the international criminal court, because -- and because we speak the same language as any international criminal court deemed of that word in the world. This is the language of criminal law, the language that everybody needs to understand. This is the language of common sense. I do not think that this criminal Tribunal in The Hague should be above other courts. I do not think that the judges and the counsel in this Tribunal should in any way be above the standards of any other serious professional in criminal law. Quite the reverse. I think that in this Tribunal, justice will be dispensed only if we, all of us who participate in this case, behave in line with the rules of our trade. And the basic rule of our trade says that the judgement must be based on evidence which is above any reasonable doubt. And how do we understand this? To my mind, it means that in the case of severest crimes, wherever in the world the decision on the guilt is taken by laymen, by jury, by jury persons, and these juries, include pensioners, car mechanics, house wives, not some superlawyers. They know what is beyond any reasonable doubt. It is what nobody doubts. An ordinary man without legal education has to know why is somebody being brought to trial, what he's accused of and why he is acquitted. This is the chief idea behind fair trial. My client is entitled to know what he is accused of and on the basis of what he is being tried. Today, before this Court, I wish to present his views, his questions, and his argument, what he has to say with regard to what he is being charged with, and I expect, answers from the Court in their judgement and my client expects to understand it. He expects a fair trial, a trial which will say, for things that have not been proven beyond reasonable doubt, he is set free, he is acquitted. As it is the position of this Defence that the Prosecutor has failed to prove any single count in the indictment beyond any reasonable doubt, let us then go through the indictment and I will speak of the doubts raised in relation to each one of the counts. In the second amended indictment of the 20th of September, 2001, the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal charges Vinko Martinovic, an HVO soldier from Mostar, with the commission of a number of crimes, crimes against humanity, grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions, violations of the laws and customs of war. In terms of their substance, these acts incorporate the persecution of Bosnian Muslims, unlawful labour, inhumane treatment of prisoners of war, torture, murder alternatively -- alternatively qualified murder, forcible transfer of Bosnian Muslims, destruction and plunder of their property. All these crimes were allegedly committed between April, 1993 and the end of January 1994 in Mostar during the armed conflict between Croats and Bosniaks in that city. Vinko Martinovic is indicted for these crimes both pursuant to the principle of responsibility of superior authority and the principle of individual criminal responsibility. The 15 months of hearings are behind us. The evidence has been produced, and we've also heard the Prosecutor's final argument. What does the accused Vinko Martinovic have to say in answer to that? What does his Defence have to say in response to that? Count 1, persecution. Under this count of the indictment, Vinko Martinovic is charged with persecutions on political, racial, and religious grounds, qualified as a crime against humanity. The acts of commission relative to this count are the crucial point of the indictment, because they practically incorporate all the other acts indicated in the indictment. And I'd like now to -- us to pause and think about this legal qualification. The Defence believes that the legal qualification under count 1 -- in count 1 is untenable in a situation when in this indictment, once again and as a separate count, we have the charges from count 1, namely the commission of this crime under count 1, that is persecutions, and it says the persecution -- the expulsion of Muslims, plunder, torture, incarceration, human shields, and the like. And after that, all this is once again qualified as separate -- as separate acts under different counts. What does that mean? It means that for one and the same act, we may be -- we may account twice. We can be punished twice, once when we call -- when we qualify a particular act as persecution and a second time when that same act is qualified as inhumane treatment and the like. And I'd like to know which is the accused whom I could explain in some sensible way that he can be punished for one and the same thing twice, and which jury would accept that? Perhaps in some systems, it could be qualified in this way, but the accused and the victims come from a system where such a thing does not exist, and that is one argument that must be heeded. The position of this Defence is that an accused before an international court may not be placed in a position which will be more difficult than would be the one if he were tried in the country where the alleged crimes were committed. We are promoting the international criminal law and I go along with that, but precisely because of that, I am appealing to you not to turn the international criminal court into an American court or some other court. I appeal to you to promote it along the principles of justice and fairness, because these are principles that everybody can understand. And we, as Defence counsel -- well, we were chosen by our client precisely because of that, so that we could defend him in a manner that he can understand, rather than find himself before a foreign court with foreign lawyers who are interpreting to him foreign jurisdiction, and he is thus left aside from his own Defence. That is, he has no manner of voicing his own defence. We think that the jurisdiction and law of the country of origin of the accused is valid for this Tribunal, that it may not be underestimated, be it when we are talking about the procedure, legal qualifications, or punishment. And therefore, the objections of the Defence go to the vagueness of the indictment of the international Prosecutor and the legal qualifications, and these objections are of a lasting nature. We firmly believe that the Court should not allow the Prosecutor to introduce in the international criminal law the practice or the system of a multiple charges, multiple counts for one and the same crime. We are still talking about this first count, the persecution, so let us see what is it that the Prosecutor highlighted in his case against Vinko Martinovic. The Prosecutor said that Vinko Martinovic played a pivotal role and that he was a generally known executor of persecutions, or as was said in the closing argument of the Prosecution, ethnic cleansing in Mostar in 1993. On the opposite side of this thesis, the Defence says that Vinko Martinovic objectively could not be that individual, nor did he take part in this. The Defence's evidence has shown that quite the contrary, Vinko Martinovic protected his Bosniak -- his Muslim neighbours against persecution. The Defence's evidence has shown that during the period referred to in the indictment, Vinko Martinovic had no military or political powers that could be related to the planning, instigating, or committing any strategic actions in Mostar, let alone in the broader area of Herzegovina. The Prosecutor has not produced a single evidence to indicate that Vinko Martinovic was anything more than a soldier on the front line who, without any rank, led a group of fellow combatants along a front line some -- about a hundred metres long. If one has that position, one cannot act strategically, one cannot instigate, one cannot encourage, one cannot engage in systematic persecution. Who is it that Vinko Martinovic met with? Who is it that he planned with? What did he plan? Whom and how did he instigate? What powers was he vested with? The Prosecutor has not answered these questions. He has offered us no proof for that particular tale. What did we hear in the Prosecutor's closing argument in this regard? The Prosecutor told us that unfortunately, this war had introduced a new term, and that is "ethnic cleansing," which ought to be synonymous with types of persecution carried out in wars which followed the disintegration of Yugoslavia. So the Prosecution's thesis is that in the Croat-Bosniak conflict in Mostar in 1993, the HVO applied the method of ethnic cleansing and that the accused Martinovic participated in it. This thesis was served to us by representatives of international organisations, people in white clothes of European monitors, who, during luncheons with leading political and military commanders of all the parties to the conflict, gathered information about the nature of the conflict. And on such occasions, they made a mistake. And that mistake is called they could not see the forest because of -- for a tree, they couldn't see a forest. They did not see that it was no -- it was not a special method but that the war which in 1991 in Croatia, and then in 1992 in Bosnia and Herzegovina, was started by Serbia, Montenegro and the JNA, that that war was actually called ethnic cleansing. The name of that war is Ethnic Cleansing. That war, that aggression, had no other purpose in mind, pursued nothing else. Everything in that war was subordinated to that goal: Ethnic cleansing. From the territories they wanted for themselves, the Serbs started expelling the non-Serb population. And in this manner, they determined the nature of the war waged in Bosnia and Herzegovina. When this process started -- once this process started, it became unstoppable. And in the spring of 1993, this war -- that war made its way to Mostar. Am I to mention here the famous decision of the Security Council of the UN, which, during the fiercest Serb aggression against the Muslims and Croats, prohibited the Muslims and Croats to purchase weapons to defend themselves? This decision was tantamount to a death sentence of thousands of Croats and Bosniaks, and told the Serbs, "Go ahead, finish your job." And so ethnic cleansing was legitimised. What perhaps was not clear then to international monitors was clear to every individual inhabitant of Bosnia-Herzegovina around whom shells were falling at that same time. That inhabitant understood perfectly that the fighting about no-man's land had started and that every one of the three peoples had to find room for itself, because that was the formula imposed by the Serbs and endorsed by the international community. It is not my intention to analyse the role of the international community but simply to point out at two different views related to persecution and ethnic cleansing. One of these views, a view from above, from the Prosecutor's Office, and a view from below, from the angle of ordinary people who survived that war and who testified here. The Prosecutor says it does not matter who started the war, we won't now talk about the Serb aggression here. But it is important, because the one who started it imposed the pattern of the war. In this count of the indictment, it is said that the persecution was carried out on the racial, ethnic, and religious grounds. The Prosecutor even says Stela hated Muslims, and the chief proof of that is that some witnesses had heard him call them "balijas." And for the Prosecutor, that is the chief proof in the eyes of the Prosecutor that there was a discriminatory intent. International experts and monitors must have come by information that Serbs, Croats, and Muslims in Bosnia hated one another and therefore killed one another. We heard witnesses from Mostar, Prosecutor's witnesses and Defence's witnesses. None of them said that Muslims, Croats, and Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina hated one another before the war, and in particular, we did not hear that in relation to Vinko Martinovic, Stela. We did not hear that he hated anyone, just because he was a Muslim or a Serb. The answer to that question, to the question about hatred in relation to a discriminatory intent, is something that every inhabitant in Bosnia-Herzegovina also knows, and the answer is not hatred but fear. The Bosniaks and the Croats did not go to war in Mostar because on the 9th of May, 1993, they started hating one another, but because an ethnic war had been raging around them for a long time by then, and because the critical amount of fear of the other had already amassed in them. They did not see then their people living next to them as their Muslim neighbours or Croat neighbours but as potential enemies. And that word, "Balija," that the Prosecutor persists in using as a -- the pivotal evidence about discriminatory behaviour needs to be demystified, Your Honours, in this courtroom, once and for all. I really got a headache listening to witnesses, Muslims and Croats alike, interpreting, explaining to this Court what the word "balija" means. And it is very simple. It is an insult. It is a word which is offensive to Muslims. And at the same time, during that same period of time, Serbs were called Chetniks, and Croats Ustasha. And these were all insults meant for Serb and Croat. And that is how insulted one another and called Serbs, Croats, and Muslims that war year of 1993. Why? Because villages and towns were ablaze around them. Can one really expect that they were to be polite at the time? A war cannot be waged from an office. One cannot forget the circumstances under which things were happening, how things looked then and how they could look now. One pretty usual insult cannot make us try somebody by an international court. In the media at the time, on all the three sides, in newspapers, on TV, these derogatory terms were used every day. I do not justify that, but I also cannot allow somebody to make a mountain out of a mole hill. Your Honours, maybe we can have a break now, and I propose to continue after the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We are still on count 1 and we are talking about the role of Vinko Martinovic, Stela, in ethnic cleansing. The Prosecutor says that Vinko Martinovic was a military commander with a key role in the persecution of Muslims in Mostar. Was it really so? What did witnesses have to say about that? Did any of the witnesses confirm that, or was it the Prosecutor who testified to that effect? Who was actually Vinko Martinovic in Mostar in 1993? Vinko Martinovic, with a rank of a foot soldier in the HVO, in a unit called Mrmak and later on Vinko Skrobo, his duty was a commander. The strength of the unit was 50 to 70 men. The task of the unit was to man the line near the medical centre and the length of that line was between 80 and 100 metres. He didn't have any other duties. He didn't have any other authority. He didn't hold any political or military positions. Did he ever attend any significant military or political meetings? He didn't. Was he a member of a political party? He wasn't. So what kind of a key role did he then have in Mostar in 1993? That is what every reasonable person would ask. There is one thing, and only one thing, that made Vinko Martinovic a key figure in Mostar in 1993, and the reason is, actually, the fact that he is here in front of an International Tribunal. So it would be good to make him responsible for everything that happened in Mostar and bring this story to an end. What is the link between that and the Jeremy Bowen's footage that we were shown by the Prosecutor? Was he filmed by a film camera, either him or his unit? Does the link arise from the fact that the footage shows persecution of Muslims? And maybe that persecution should be ascribed to Vinko Martinovic? How is the link established between him and hundreds of nameless victims, expelled people, the photos of the families who were victimised by the war? Where is evidence proving that -- has Vinko Martinovic brought before this Tribunal to be found responsible for everything that happened in Mostar? He is here to seek justice. He is here of his own will. He has been promised a fair trial, and this is what he requests. He demands to be tried based on evidence. The Prosecutor himself, in his closing argument, gave us 17 highest-ranking military commanders who made decisions in Mostar in 1993. The Prosecutor gave us the entire structure of the HVO. He explained to us the political background of military activities that took place during the conflict in Mostar. Among those names, he didn't mention the name of Vinko Martinovic. Amongst the thousands of documents relative to the political and military power in which different persons are mentioned, there is no name of Vinko Martinovic. How come, then, that he is so important? What makes him so important? What brings him here to this Tribunal? Vinko Martinovic is here because he is not important, because he was never important, because he doesn't have any military or political protectors or sponsors. And because of that fact that he is not important, he was the scape-goat when somebody had to be sent to The Hague. And now, what about the persecution of Bosniaks and Muslims in Mostar in 1993? In the final brief, we have put forth our positions and we said that Mostar, at the relevant time, was the place where a number of refugees came, and we put forth the thesis according to which these newly arrived refugees were the ones who carried out persecutions on both banks of the river in Mostar. I don't have the time to belabour on that, but you will find that in our final brief. Our -- according to our thesis, there was no need for any particular plan or order, ordering persecution, but rather that the perpetrator of the persecution were the same people who had experienced the same thing in their native villages. They had seen how this was done and now, in the same way that they had once been expelled, they started expelling others. I would like to dwell upon the testimonies of Muslims, MA, MB, MC, MD, ME, MF, MG, MH, MI, MK, and others. This I don't want to state for the record, because the Prosecutor himself mentioned all these witnesses as "some" witnesses. What did these witnesses have to say to us? Those people were Muslims from the west part of Mostar, who were visited by unknown groups of criminals who knocked on their doors in order to evict them from their apartments. They all said one and same thing. They said that they were expelled by people unknown to them, unknown because they were not from Mostar, because it was war which had brought them to Mostar. They had never seen them before. The witnesses said that their neighbour Vinko Martinovic had protected them, that they knew him as a person who didn't make a distinction between Croats, Muslims, and Serbs. Why did they turn to him for protection? Because he was the only soldier for whom they believed that he would not leave them out in the cold, that they could turn to him for help, that he was brave and strong, and that he was ready to engage his physical strength, the strength of his unit, to protect his Muslim neighbours. How did he help them? He would come, together with his soldiers, to protect them from those who wanted to evict them. He would give them documents of his unit so that they could introduce themselves as persons engaged in the HVO and that they could thus regulate some of their affairs. He would go to other parts of the city to save members of these people's family from persecution. Witness MA and his family hid in the house of Martinovic's parents, and he helped Muslims with money and with food that he gave them. At their request, he would help them to join with their families who lived in other parts of the town. He would help them if they wanted to leave Mostar and go to other towns or to other countries. Vinko Martinovic, in the situation where he found himself, against his own will, in Mostar, in 1993, did the only possible thing. Every day, he helped his neighbours, his Muslim neighbours, as much as he possibly could. He couldn't help everybody, but in his neighbourhood, in the part of town called Balinovac, owing to him, the most Muslims have remained, and they personally came to this Court to explain how Vinko Martinovic had helped them, when he had helped them, and we have all of their initials in our final brief. Who were these witnesses? Who were these Muslims who testified here? They were ordinary people, neighbours, from whom Vinko Martinovic could not expect any favours in return. Nobody showed any interest in them. Nobody could protect them. Nobody could help them out of the dire straits. Nobody wanted to help them. And they themselves could not find an escape from the situation that was so difficult for them. And what did the Prosecutor have to say to all this evidence? He ignored it, as if this evidence didn't exist, as if it wasn't important -- even as if it wasn't a mitigating circumstance. Nothing. And all this was very important for these people and it maybe even saved their lives. I believe that this Trial Chamber will find their testimonies important. Can we say that things didn't happen the way these people testified? After their testimonies, can we say that Vinko Martinovic systematically persecuted civilians, Bosniak Muslims, on religious grounds? Was it Vinko Martinovic who did that when he hid a Muslim family in the basement of his parents' house? Was it Vinko Martinovic who did that when, during the most fierce conflict, organised a Muslim burial of his neighbour's mother, at the time when such a thing was absolutely inconceivable? Vinko Martinovic, for whom MA, MB, MC, MD, MF, and MH said that he protected them and saved them. The Defence presented a lot of evidence with regard to this count, which shows that the name of Vinko Martinovic, i.e., his nickname Stela, was used to disguise the real perpetrators of plunder and other crimes. This is the way the Defence wants to answer, to rely to, the testimonies of Prosecutor's witnesses who spoke about the role of Vinko Martinovic in persecutions, i.e., of the participation of his soldiers in that persecution. Since my colleague, Mr. Seric, has already spoken about that misrepresentation, I will not dwell upon that. I'm just going to point out the Exhibit P626, in which we could see -- and the exhibit was a SIS report -- in which we could see that many a group of criminals were falsely introducing themselves by the name of Stelici. After that, we also saw proposals as to how this should be prevented. And we also heard testimonies by Muslim witnesses to that effect, who told us about things that they had seen personally when groups of criminals came knocking on their doors and falsely presenting themselves. For example, a witness was describing a situation when Stela was personally present in his apartment, when soldiers came knocking to the door of that apartment, introducing themselves as members of his unit. Witnesses were talking about situations when some refugees came and said that it was Stela who had expelled them, and they said in Stela's presence, so the person who had introduced himself as Stela actually abused Stela's name. So these witnesses explained to us why was Stela's name so suitable for somebody to say, "I am Stela," or, "I am a Stelici." It was because he was famous for his bravery and strength. His name became famous during the war with -- against the Serbs. So it was widely believed that a mere mention of his name would produce a desired effect. That is, either somebody would get really scared or they wouldn't dare verify the introduction. There are more details of that in our final brief. But what I would like to emphasise at this point is the fact that this count of the indictment charges the -- Vinko Martinovic with command responsibility, and this is what the Prosecutor did during his case. He mentioned the instances when Stela's soldiers were seen as participants in plunder and persecution. In no such case did the Prosecutor establish a link between the alleged events and Vinko Martinovic himself. We believe that in such a situation, Vinko Martinovic cannot be held responsible and charged with command responsibility if something did not exist in his consciousness, if he didn't know that things were happening, if he could not know that was happening, and if he didn't have a duty to know that things were happening. Maybe we could illustrate that with an example. Let's take, for example, a modern army, NATO, for example, and if, for example, a soldier, a NATO soldier, whose name for this purpose will be James Smith, has an afternoon off. He leaves his barracks, goes to a pub or a bar wearing his uniform, gets drunk, and there rapes a girl, whose initials for this purpose will be MN. Will his commander - let's call him Miller - who had stayed in the barracks, so will he be charged with that rape as his commander? So will he be charged with command responsibility? I don't believe so. Let's now replace the names with some other names. Instead of NATO, let's use the HVO. Instead of Smith, let's use Ernest Takac. And instead of commander Miller, let's say commander Martinovic. Should Martinovic be held responsible for something that Miller is not responsible for? Should the legal situation be the same? It is the position of this Defence that command responsibility is not an objective responsibility, and that Vinko Martinovic should not be held responsible for the things possibly committed by his soldiers during their time off, the things that he didn't know anything about and was not in the position to know anything about. Since I do not have much time, perhaps I will not be able to address all counts individually so that I'm moving to the 17th of September, 1993, wooden rifles. The rest, the previous counts, they are in the closing brief. If I have time, I'll come back to they will. Ergo, counts 2 to 8. The date, 17th of September, 1993. The indictment says Vinko Martinovic ordered to issue the prisoners with wooden rifles and they were to move next to the tank, and we discussed it here for several months. It is the Defence's position that the story about the wooden rifles, which allegedly were given to prisoners of war, was a story that was told in Mostar and in Bosnia in relation to different locations, central Bosnia, Santiceva Street in Mostar, and also witnesses have told us it was transmitted, told and retold by those incarcerated at the Heliodrom, via media, without ever being associated with Vinko Martinovic and his unit. It was only when the proceedings were launched against Vinko Martinovic that somebody tried to link this story with Vinko Martinovic. The Prosecutor mostly refers to a document P608, about a combat action on 17th of September, and the testimonies of LP, JJ and the investigators who have allegedly found a wooden rifle, which again allegedly was used in that action. The Defence's position is that the wooden rifle incident did not happen in Vinko Martinovic's unit. When Witness PP was testify -- testified, he said that there were a number of incidents involving wooden rifles. Witness AF stated to Apolonia Bos, investigator of the Prosecutor, that prisoners with wooden rifles were on Santiceva Street outside Martinovic's area of responsibility. This investigator confirmed it during her testimony before this Chamber. During the testimony of the Prosecution's witness Allan Knudsen, a question was put about a number of incidents where prisoners were issued with wooden rifles. Witnesses PP and OO mentioned different dates on which that incident had taken place. Document P608 says SIS report, secret police. There was an operation on the 17th of September, 1993, and the order was issued to Vinko Martinovic. The Prosecutor's document says Vinko Martinovic refused to command the commander Mario Milicevic, Baja. The Defence says Vinko Martinovic does not have the command responsibility on Bulevar on the 17th of September, nor was he in command. Document P612.1 says -- it's a Prosecutor's document -- all individuals who on the 17th of September, 1993, were sent from the Heliodrom to Vinko Skrobo, all returned on the 27th of September, 1993, to the Heliodrom. This document is dated 28th of September, 1993, and it tallies with information from the Heliodrom, that is the information found in logbooks for the date of the 17th of September. There are the names of prisoners sent to work at Vinko Skrobo unit on the 17th of September. So the documents of the Prosecution referring to these incidents, they speak about wooden rifles, about the command responsibility of Vinko Martinovic on Bulevar and so on and so on, but these documents tell us the contrary to what the Prosecution sets out to prove. And what does the Prosecutor respond to that? He simply says document P612.1 is false. That is what the Prosecutor told us in his closing argument. Now, we ask ourselves: Who brought this false document to the Court? The answer: The Prosecutor. Who here tried to persuade us that this and other documents were authentic? The Prosecution's investigator as a witness in this case. How is it that only now, in the closing argument, we hear from the Prosecutor that a particular document is false? Can we be told which other documents are also false too in these 17 binders? Doesn't the Defence have the right to say what is false are the allegations of the Prosecution's witnesses, Allan Knudsen, OO, PP, JJ testifying about these facts. Can the Defence say, "Witness OO lied when he said there was a wooden rifle in the museum," because we have established that that is not true. Can the Defence say, "The wooden rifle brought by the investigator of the Prosecution -- brought because this rifle was planted by AID?" Can we say that the witnesses for the Prosecution a currently two active officers in the BH Army, a foreign mercenary and the Prosecution's investigator, and that is why we don't believe them? The indictment claims that prisoners of war with wooden rifles were forced to walk along the tank which was moving towards the enemy positions and the purpose of this operation, said the Prosecutor, was to provoke the fire from the positions of the BH Army, to open fire on disguised prisoners so that the HVO man in the tank could identify, could see where the enemy positions were. And it suffices to look at the photograph of the Bulevar to understand that such claims lack any ground whatsoever. What we are talking about is the separation line on the Bulevar where, on one side of this line, there are the HVO positions in fortified buildings and on the other side of that same street, called Bulevar, are the positions of the BH Army in fortified buildings. The distance between them? 20 to 50 metres. And that line remains unchanged for several months prior to this event. Soldiers on one side know all the positions of the soldiers on the other side. They know one another. They call to each other. They negotiate. And it goes on and on for months on end. And how, then, can we make ourselves believe that it was exactly on the 17th of September, 1993, that it became unknown where the enemy's position -- where the enemy positions were. And they needed to be identified in this manner to allow the tank to go into action. The tank which is intended to destroy buildings, and which was the reason why it had come to the Bulevar, to fire on fortified buildings. The explanation about the human shield, about the reasons -- the reasons of the -- to explain why the prisoners were made to walk next to a tank -- beggars, any reasonable explanation, and the whole story about wooden rifles doesn't hold water. I do not have time to talk about the wooden rifle which we received during the rebuttal case, and what we think about such an unacceptable exhibit. We said in our closing argument, and the Chamber has also had the opportunity to see it at the time when this evidence, this type of evidence, was produced. Wooden rifles -- I won't waste time with them anymore. But in that same count, there is something which surfaced only during the closing argument, and -- but that is something that I must not forget. Namely, having closed his case, the Prosecutor decided to withdraw the charge for the human shield, in which allegedly three prisoners were killed. And the Court has then decided that the Prosecution has failed to prove this charge about the human shield in the area of Vinko Skrobo unit. Nevertheless, in their closing argument, they mention the responsibility of Vinko Martinovic for the death of Aziz Colakovic and Enis Pajo who, according to the witness for the Prosecution, were killed in a section of the Bulevar next to the dugout trenches. That is in the area of the civilian police, not next to the health centre where the area of responsibility of Vinko Martinovic was. And precisely for that reason that it was known that those two men had not been killed in Vinko Martinovic's area of responsibility, the Prosecutor withdrew his charge for human shield. But now tries, through the back door, to introduce once again two more dead souls, even though he knows that they were not killed in Vinko Martinovic's area of responsibility. But he nevertheless tries to add yet another charge. The wounding of Senad Pajo was addressed in a similar manner. In a document P5662 [as interpreted], item 2, it is said that that wounded prisoner, Senad Pajo was taken away by Dinko Kenezovic from the Heliodrom in some direction. It doesn't say where. He was taken away by Dinko Kenezovic. We all know that Dinko Kenezovic is Vinko Martinovic's soldier. And so the Prosecutor says since Dinko is Vinko's soldier, and since he took Pajo away, then he must have taken him to Vinko and that is where he was wounded then. Perhaps we could even make -- bring ourselves to believe that, had that same Prosecutor not said something completely contrary to this in his closing argument, and that is what he did. Witness AF was taken to Stela's unit, to Vinko Martinovic's, although he was taken to that unit by soldier Luka Stojanovski who was a member of the military police. And then the Prosecutor affirmed it does not matter from which unit does this soldier who drives prisoners come; he can take them to any unit. Yes, he can. But then, couldn't Dinko Kenezovic, couldn't he have taken Enes Pajo to some other unit? Is that beyond reasonable doubt? And how is it that one and the same document is interpreted in two completely different ways? In counts of the indictment, you're referring to the manner in which prisoners were used to work along the separation line, the Prosecutor told us in his closing argument that it is a sensible conclusion, I guess on the basis of all that we heard during there case, forgetting that a number of witnesses, soldiers, and especially prisoners -- Muslim prisoners of war, who testified here about how they fared, they said that they were never prisoners on the front line. However, we now use a different pair of eyes to look at that. And the Prosecutor says, and it is a common sense conclusion that Vinko Martinovic used prisoners to work on the front line so as not to expose his soldiers to danger. Is that proof? Are such constructs a proof? And I wouldn't have even mentioned it hadn't, in another place, in the Harmandic case, the Prosecutor continued along the same -- in the same vein and says it is logical to conclude that it was easier for Vinko Martinovic to let Harmandic be killed or to kill him than to take him back to the Heliodrom beaten up. What are such claims based on? The Prosecutor knows that it cannot serve as a proof. But at the same time, he seizes the opportunity to represent Vinko Martinovic as a criminal and to suggest that he had some ideas in his head which are merely the figment of the Prosecutor's imagination, and that is not permissible. That is not done. I will have to move to the count involving Harmandic but before that, I must tell the Court that in so far as the stay of prisoners -- in so far as the prisoners were concerned, they should look at our closing brief, what we had to say about that. I wish to underline that there were a number of Muslim witnesses, witnesses who were prisoners of war, who described to us how they had fared with Vinko Martinovic, Stela. And what did they tell us? All of them said, "We felt much safer in that unit than in other units, safer than at the Heliodrom." They said, "We begged Vinko Martinovic to ask us to come to work in his unit so as not to be taken to other units." They stated that they had their meals in the lad Vina restaurant together with the soldiers of the unit, that they moved about without any guards or escort, that they went home to see their families, that they went to have a bath and for a change of clothes, that they were paid for certain jobs in kind, be it food or cigarettes. They said that none of the prisoners were killed or wounded, that the physical labour around the separation area were performed under conditions that were not life-threatening. That is perhaps a characteristics statement of Witness ME who described how Vinko Martinovic had helped me -- helped him to get out of detention and to leave together with his family for a third country. This witness described to us how Vinko Martinovic had hidden him in a house before he left Mostar, that he had even supplied him with a weapon and ammunition for his personal protection, and that he had undertaken everything to help this witness to put through his plan to get rid of the imprisonment and go abroad. This witness said that literally before this Chamber that Vinko Martinovic had saved his life. Counts 13 to 18, Harmandic, alternative qualification, the Prosecutor says manslaughter, if not then, then torture, battery. The Defence's position, we object to this qualification for a simple reason: The accused must know what he's being accused of. Is it manslaughter or is itself ear injury? He has to know it because that will determine his defence. I do not have time to go through that, but I point out once again we cannot have alternative qualifications and because this makes us infer that the Prosecutor is not really sure about what he wants to say. We know the whole story. A former policeman, according to the indictment, was brought to Vinko Martinovic's unit and vanished. The Prosecutor says perhaps he was killed, and perhaps he wasn't, but there is no doubt that he was beaten up. The Defence says Harmandic was brought to the unit; Vinko Skrobo, on the 12th of July, 1993. When he came, he was already beaten when he came there because he had been beaten at the Heliodrom, both by prisoners and by policemen. Proof, Prosecution's witnesses AD and AE, and they confirm what? They confirm that he was beaten up at the Heliodrom. So what is our thesis founded on? On Prosecution's evidence, documents, P434, order for the release of prisoners of war to go to work. Under 37, one can see the order issued to send prisoners to work, and the person who took prisoners out on the 13th of July, 1993, was Miljenko Cule. Cule, the commander of the first light assault battalion of the military police. Why is the 13th of July important? Because we say that the 12th of July he was at Stela's and returned and now somebody takes him out from the Heliodrom on the 13th. Who is it? Miljenko Cule. The first light assault military -- battalion of the military police, document P434. Document PP520 is a list of some prisoners from the Heliodrom and the comment where they were taken and who took them. Under number one, we see Nenad Harmandic, where he was taken; the first light assault; the date, 13th of July, 1993; who takes him there, Miljenko Cule. These documents show that the prisoner of war, Nenad Harmandic was taken on the 13th of July, 1993, from the Heliodrom, by a member of the 1st Light Assault Battalion, Miljenko Cule. The Prosecutor's Exhibit P774, the report on the death of prisoners of war, under 56, and the subtitle is "List of Escaped Prisoners of War," the first name on that list, Nenad Harmandic. Another document which we received from the Prosecutor, it also has the Defence number D2/14, special SIS report, the secret police, about the information relative to the escape of Muslim prisoners from the Heliodrom. Under number 15, it says a soldier of the 1st Light Assault, Miljenko Cule, took Nenad Harmandic to work and the latter escaped. So these documents are self-explanatory and they tell us that on the 13th of July, 1993, Nenad Harmandic was taken from the Heliodrom for work, a member of the 1st Light Assault Battalion, Miljenko Cule, and Nenad Harmandic escaped. In other words, according to these documents, nobody was killed, nobody was wounded, nobody was abused. There is no Vinko Skrobo ATG and no Vinko Martinovic. The Prosecution presented exhibits, Witness AD obviously is concerned with Harmandic's lot, and she stated on the 12th of July, 1993, I saw Nenad Harmandic in the Vinko Skrobo unit, and I heard that on the same day, he was returned to the Heliodrom. And this is exactly what the Defence claims. Nenad Harmandic was brought to the Vinko Skrobo unit on the 12th of July, 1993, and was returned to the Heliodrom on the same day. On the following day, on the 13th of July, 1993, Miljenko Cule took him from the Heliodrom to the 1st Light Assault and from then, Nenad Harmandic escaped. The military police believes that it had been prearranged by him and Miljenko Cule, we conclude that from the SIS report which speaks about the way the escape was organised. So the Prosecutor's witness and the Prosecutor exhibit give an answer to the question as to how Nenad Harmandic disappeared. But now we have an alternative qualification. If he was not murdered, then let's say that he was beaten up. Evidence to prove that are Prosecutor's exhibits and testimonies by Halil Ajanic, by Witness AD and AE, by Witnesses AF and AM and by forensic expert Dr. Zujo. The only key witness is Halil Ajanic. He allegedly saw what happened, and he was here to testify to how Nenad Harmandic had been beaten up. According to Ajanic -- actually about his testimony, we can say that he is the person suffering from alcoholic psychosis, that he has amnestic syndrome, and that he suffers from epilepsy. And we learned that from the testimony of Dragan Begic, who is a psychiatric expert, who testified here, and who explained in very great detail the quality of that testimony. And he also said that the reliability of a testimony given by such a witness is very dubious, that they cannot be trusted when they provide information because they more often than not do not speak the truth. Witnesses AD and AE do not have any personal knowledge about the destiny of Harmandic. AD allegedly learned about the destiny of Harmandic from AF, and following that conversation, an exhumation was carried out in order to identify Harmandic's body. The Prosecutor's witness AF denies any such conversation had taken place and that he had provided AE with any such information. So one Prosecutor's witness completely contradicted another Prosecutor's witness. AF and AN testified as Prosecutor's witnesses, and they said they had buried a body which could have been Harmandic's body. But none of them were able to claim that for a fact. AF did not know Nenad Harmandic. Witness M said he didn't know who was it that he had buried. And they also told us the story about two different events. So again we are faced with a situation that the Prosecutor gives us another alternative, for us to decide who was it that actually had buried the body. The forensic expert Zujo participated in the exhumation of bodies in Liska Park in Mostar, and he allegedly identified Harmandic's according to the data provided by the family. This has been disputed by the Defence, this expert testimony has been disputed. A new expertise was given by Dr. Josip Skavic and what did Skavic tell us? Exhibit D2/25, Dr. Skavic told us, "In the identification of the body of NN, under number 5, I found -- came across a number of elements which make it implausible that the body belonged to Nenad Harmandic." The elements that he mentioned was an error in the height, the identification by clothing disputable. Prosecutor's witnesses AF and M claim, for example, that Harmandic had last been seen wearing white shorts. During the identification the body was found to be wearing a pair of blue jeans. AF said that everybody's lighters had been taken away at the Heliodrom. During the identification, a lighter and a leather belt were found on the body. So these are the disputable facts. The identification based on the projectile which was found by the body was disputed because Zujo could not say where the projectile was found. So it is common knowledge that Nenad Harmandic, unfortunately, is still missing. Documents say that he went missing on the 13th of July, 1993, from the 1st Light Assault Battalion of the military police, where he had been brought by Miljenko Cule. Maybe this is the lead that should have been followed up in order to establish the destiny of Nenad Harmandic. There were quite a number of hearsay testimonies by the detainees who had heard about Nenad Harmandic and who testified about these stories before this Court. The only problem is that this is all hearsay, which originates from the same source, and it is Halil Ajanic. He is the one who told the story at the Heliodrom. The story was then retold and ended up in the courtroom. So Halil Ajanic is the source of all this hearsay, and the -- a psychiatrist told us about the quality of Halil Ajanic's testimony. I do not have the time to belabour on other counts of the indictment. I would just like to say something about the Vinko Skrobo unit that -- because we believe that it is very important to establish the area of responsibility of that unit so as to avoid a situation in which Vinko Martinovic would be held responsible for something that happened beyond that area of responsibility. We also believe that it is very important to establish the time when that unit was established, because we claim that on the 9th of May, Vinko Martinovic was not the commander of that unit, that that unit did not exist on that day, and he cannot be charged with the possible persecution on that day. The unit was established later on. Everything I didn't have the time to say in my closing argument one can find in our final brief, and I kindly ask the Chamber to read it. So in summarising all this, I would like to say that the Prosecutor has failed to prove beyond all reasonable doubt any of the counts in the indictment against Vinko Martinovic, and based on that, the Prosecution (sic) suggests that the Trial Chamber should find Vinko Martinovic not guilty on all the counts of the indictment and release him from custody. This was all from the Defence. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Par. Pursuant to Rule 86 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, tomorrow morning we will have the rebuttal argument. I would like to remind both parties that in this respect, this Tribunal has adopted very strict criteria for this procedure. According to the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, the rebuttal argument must be related to the significant issues arising directly out of the Defence final brief and closing argument which could not reasonably have been anticipated. The Prosecution could not repeat what has already been said in its final brief and closing argument, with the sole purpose to reinforce its case. This test will apply equally to the Defence team, with the understanding that the Defence have already rebutted some points in the Prosecution's final brief and closing argument yesterday and today. Therefore, each party will have more or less one hour for its rebuttal or rejoinder argument tomorrow. Having said that, we will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00, in the same courtroom.
